World of Warcraft: Legion First Impressions

I feel a bit lost. This is the first expansion in wow that I've been able to read about and find that I just don't care anymore. I loved this game, I spent months of my life playing it in every facet possible, but now I find myself completed uninterested. It seems Warlords must have been the last straw.

I suppose it's not such a massive surprise, I think I knew when I unsubscribed last that there was no mental reservation that it would only be for a while, I guess I knew I was done. Still sad though, to see something you used to be passionate about raising not even a blip of a interest.

They're saying all the right things. But it's all going to come down to the execution. Will they follow through on their promises? Will they be as dedicated to Legion when it's been out for six months as they are now, or will they abandon it after one content patch with eyes on the next payday, as they did with WoD?

I choose to be optimistic, but guardedly so.

I find the addition of class halls encouraging. I've been playing on and off since Vanilla and have been saddened how every class has been homogenized. I remember doing the quests to make my pally weapon, Verigan's Fist, and the epic mount quest, and doing the epic mount quests on my warlock. Taming and training various beasts on my hunter, to learn new pet abilities to pass on to your own pet.

I remember me and a friend taking our hunters into LBRS with invisibility potions etc to get to the bottom of the dungeon to get to the wargs. You had to tame one of them so you could learn Bite - Rank 8, the only source in the game. It was a blast. All these things made each class unique and made doing them give me a real sense of accomplishment.

The point is it was difficult, it took effort, some skill and research to maximise your abilities, and also lots of play to hone your skills, in other words, it was a game that you got better at the harder you tried. Now you can be as good as you need to be by just turning up. It's like dating. One has to break their back to be as good as they can be to succeed, the other just has to be in the right place wearing the right clothes.

I'm guardedly optimistic. But they had better nail it this time, because after WoD I'm almost done with it. And wings. Wings. WINGS, and no not the garlic parmesan variety. I have heard nothing about flying, and as of this post there's still no flying in Draenor.

The most recent PTR patch is a release candidate so if nothing goes wrong with the stupid ashran band-aid they will most likely release it within the next week or so.

Their mistake was putting the pvp 'fix' in the same patch as the flying.

If they deliver what they announced, this could be a really amazing expansion. We finally get the Path of the Titans (now called Artifact Weapons). Class Orders sound like what garrison's should've been - especially the champions. We're back to a story that builds on the lore.

And we get not only the long promised moose, but moose Tauren!

I am looking forward to it, hope they can follow through with all their promises.

EFF Finally Gets to Ask Appeals Court to Look at 4th Amendment Question Over NSA's Backbone Sniffing

Source

It's taken many years, but one of the EFF's longstanding cases against the NSA has finally reached an important milestone: exploring the 4th Amendment question raised by the NSA tapping the internet backbone. This is part of the Jewel v. NSA case that has been going on for years. Back in February (after a lot of procedural back and forth on other issues), the district court rejected the 4th Amendment argument, basically toeing the government's "but... but... national security!" line. Not surprisingly, the EFF disagreed with the court and appealed to the 9th Circuit appeals court.

The appeal is not just about the 4th Amendment question, but also about the question of standing. Like many surveillance cases, the courts have given the government a bit of a "get out of jail free" card by not letting anyone sue unless they can prove that they, specifically, were swept up by the surveillance. The lower court used this to reject the EFF's case as well, arguing that the evidence it presented was too "speculative." On appeal, the EFF argues this is ridiculous, as you can see in the EFF's opening brief:

First, the court erred in concluding plaintiffs lacked standing. Plaintiffs’ evidence, including extensive government admissions, shows that at least some of their Internet communications have been intercepted, copied, and searched, thus establishing their injury and giving them standing. Moreover, because the government defendants put in no evidence creating a genuine factual dispute regarding plaintiffs’ standing, plaintiffs are entitled to summary judgment on standing.

And then we get to the meat of the 4th Amendment argument:

Above all, the evidence demonstrates that plaintiffs are entitled to summary judgment on the merits of their Fourth Amendment claim. The suspicionless, warrantless interception and copying of plaintiffs’ Internet communications is an unconstitutional seizure, and the subsequent content searching of some of those communications is an unconstitutional search.

Later, the EFF filing leans heavily on last year's Supreme Court ruling in the Riley case which found mobile phone searches without a warrant to be a 4th Amendment violation:

The Supreme Court recently affirmed that the government’s search and seizure of digital information implicates core Fourth Amendment values and triggers the warrant requirement. Riley, 134 S.Ct. at 2495 (“The fact that technology now allows an individual to carry such information in his hand does not make the information any less worthy of the protection for which the Founders fought.”).

The Court specifically noted the protected privacy interests in Internet browsing: “Internet search and browsing history...could reveal an individual’s private interests or concerns—perhaps a search for certain symptoms of disease, coupled with frequent visits to WebMD.” ....The Court went on to detail how a person’s digital information because of its breadth and depth gives a wide-ranging picture of a person’s most private thoughts and actions—even beyond what a general search of their home might reveal....

The Fourth Amendment privacy interests in digital information that the Supreme Court recognized in Riley are fully applicable to the Internet activities of plaintiffs that the government is seizing and searching— including emails, web browsing and searching, live chat, voice calls, social networking, photos, and videos—because of “all they contain and all they may reveal.”...

Indeed, the Court noted that much of the digital information it protected in Riley is increasingly not stored on smartphones themselves but in the Internet “cloud,” with phones used to access the information over the Internet.... Because communications between smartphones and the Internet “cloud” often transit the Internet backbone, those communications are subject to the NSA’s interception.

There's a lot more in the filing that is well worth reading, and you can expect the Justice Department to attack basically all of it. Hopefully the 9th Circuit sees through it and recognizes the core principles at play here.

It is difficult to believe that when the Founders drafted the 4th Amendment, that they didn't think it applied to sniffing up basically every communication "just in case."

I'm on day 4 of my switch from Verizon for a Google and I thought I'd share a few of my experiences.

  • First and foremost, I don't really notice any difference on a day to day basis when it comes call quality. My phone works as a phone.

  • While some folks have complained about the battery on the Nexus 6, my experiences is that it is more than offset by the fact that my Nexus isn't constantly searching for cellular signals in my office. Our building is largely lined with modern glass that seems to reflect all cell phone signals. My phone used to just burn through it's battery during the day hunting for a signal. This no longer happens.

  • My only complaint on setting up the phone was the numerous updates required to get the phone working. Out of the box, the "Fi" app claimed it was not compatible with my phone. After a few hours of panic, I realized it was actually complaining about the version of the OS, not the phone itself. 3 Android OS updates later and my phone seemed quite happy to install "Fi".

  • I'm a little sad to see some of the Google Voice features such as phone screening functionality disappear. However, I look to be saving something like $80 a month on my phone bill... ;-)

My wife and I spent a bit of timing thinking through the implications of one of us switching to Google Fi. Did we really need two phones any more? Would a single phone and an android tablet (or two) suffice with the added functionality that Google Fi gives us? In the end we chose not to use a single number yet. Google Fi is more like giving you a single floating entity than a traditional phone that could be easily shared. My wife is eagerly anticipating her invitation as we speak.
